question_text: Solve (1 + x²)dy/dx + y = e to the power Tan⁻¹x.

insider_note: The integrating factor e to the power Tan⁻¹x multiplies the right side to give e to the power 2Tan⁻¹x, so the substitution t = Tan⁻¹x is what turns the final integral into a plain ∫e²ᵗdt rather than something left in x.

steps.label: Rewrite in standard form and identify P
steps.margin_note: One mark. Divide by (1 + x²) to reach the standard linear form.
steps.memory_tip: ∫1/(1+x²) dx = Tan⁻¹x — one of the standard integrals worth remembering.

lines.text: \text{Given D.E is }\ (1 + x^{2})dy/dx + y = e^{\operatorname{Tan}^{-1} x}
\Rightarrow dy/dx + y\cdot (1/(1 + x^{2})) = e^{\operatorname{Tan}^{-1} x}/(1 + x^{2})

lines: This is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x).
steps.why: Dividing every term by (1 + x²) makes the coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1, matching the standard linear form, and the resulting P is exactly the standard derivative-of-arctan integral.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide the right side e to the power Tan⁻¹x by (1 + x²) as well as the left side.
Confusing ∫1/(1+x²)dx with ∫1/√(1−x²)dx, which gives Sin⁻¹x instead.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e to the power ∫P dx always.
steps.memory_tip: Unlike the trig examples earlier in this chapter, this I.F. does not simplify further — e to the power Tan⁻¹x is already in its simplest form.

lines.text: \therefore \text{ I.F. }\ = e^{\int P dx} = e^{\operatorname{Tan}^{-1} x}

steps.why: Since ∫P dx = Tan⁻¹x here rather than a log expression, the integrating factor e to the power Tan⁻¹x does not simplify any further — it stays exactly as it is.
common_mistakes: Trying to simplify e to the power Tan⁻¹x further, as if it were e raised to a log.
Writing the I.F. as Tan⁻¹x, forgetting that it must be e to the power Tan⁻¹x.

steps.label: Set up the integral and substitute
steps.margin_note: One mark. Multiplying two copies of e to the power Tan⁻¹x together gives e to the power 2Tan⁻¹x; the substitution t = Tan⁻¹x then removes the awkward exponent from the integral.
steps.memory_tip: e to the power A, times e to the power A, is e to the power 2A — combine matching exponentials before attempting the integral.
lines: Hence the solution is y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx
Put Tan⁻¹x = t ⇒ 1/(1 + x²) dx = dt,
steps.why: Multiplying the integrating factor by Q combines the two exponential terms into e to the power 2Tan⁻¹x, and substituting t = Tan⁻¹x removes the arctan from the exponent entirely, using the fact that dt is exactly the leftover 1/(1+x²)dx.
common_mistakes: Adding the exponents incorrectly: e to the power (Tan⁻¹x + Tan⁻¹x) must become e to the power 2Tan⁻¹x.
Forgetting that dt = 1/(1+x²) dx already matches the leftover factor exactly, and trying to substitute a different piece.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. ∫e²ᵗdt = (1/2)e²ᵗ, then substitute t = Tan⁻¹x back in.
steps.memory_tip: ∫eᵏᵗdt = eᵏᵗ/k for any constant k — here k = 2.
lines: and putting t = Tan⁻¹x back in:
steps.why: The standard rule for integrating an exponential of a constant multiple of t gives (1/2)e²ᵗ, and substituting t = Tan⁻¹x back in returns the final relation to the original variable x.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the 1/2 factor that comes from integrating e²ᵗ rather than eᵗ.
Leaving the final answer in terms of t instead of substituting Tan⁻¹x back in.
